topic: adaptive inference; early exit; distribution shift; edge systems
status: cross-period evidence synthesis; matched evaluation and global novelty unresolved
claim: Across the 2018 sampled SDN paper, the 2022 corruption-shift study, the 2025 sampled Infer-EDGE system paper, and the 2026 DART follow-up, adaptive inference savings depend on deployable exit selection, calibration under the evaluation distribution, model family, and the accounting boundary. In the 2018 and 2022 papers, label-aware first-correct exits are much better than practical confidence/patience/nearest-neighbor routes; under common corruptions, practical routes save compute but gain only about 1 accuracy point over the final exit, and the practical-oracle gap widens by about 5 points. A 2026 difficulty-aware method obtains CNN speedups with architecture-dependent accuracy costs and substantial LeViT losses in some settings. The sampled edge paper reports large selected latency/device-energy gains but excludes server and video-capture energy and simulates UAV mobility energy. These are not comparable effect estimates; together they expose a concrete, testable gap in jointly evaluating accuracy, shift, controller behavior, and complete system cost.

transformer-specific limitation and absence of edge-hardware validation

interpretation: Oracle outcomes use ground-truth correctness and are unattainable at inference; retain them only as upper bounds. The 2022 result is restricted to common image corruptions, CIFAR-10/100-C, and VGG16/ResNet56. DART's A100 benchmark does not establish edge energy. Infer-EDGE's energy accounting excludes material components and its earlier EdgeRL preprint substantially overlaps, so those versions count as one research line. Differences in datasets, controller, hardware, and metrics prohibit quantitative pooling.
falsifiable_question: Under a matched tuning/data/compute budget, do calibrated-confidence, failure-probability, and difficulty-adaptive controllers preserve accuracy while reducing compute on both clean and shifted data across CNNs and ViTs—and do those rankings survive complete device-plus-server energy and tail-latency accounting?
primary_outcome: Joint per-example exit correctness and depth; accuracy/outage and risk-coverage; FLOPs; mean and tail latency; energy measured separately for device, camera, communication, and server; performance across clean, corruption, and semantic/domain-shift sets.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The 2018 practical confidence exits do reduce CIFAR compute substantially in the reported setups; the concern is not that early exit never works.
The 2022 paper finds practical exits still reduce compute under common corruption and AugMix improves the measured calibration/exit behavior.
The 2018 oracle uses label knowledge and cannot be interpreted as deployed performance.
DART shows favorable speedups on some CNN settings and MNIST; it is not uniformly harmful.
LeViT losses and A100-only measurements limit claims about transformer and edge deployment generality.
Infer-EDGE omits server and video-capture energy and simulates UAV mobility energy; its 2024 related preprint is not independent evidence.
The 2026 ICML paper Rethinking Calibration for Early-Exit Neural Networks is verified at abstract level only in this pass; its full text remains to be audited.

confidence.oracle_vs_deployable_gap_is_important: high within the audited CNN papers

suggested_design: Use shared multi-exit CNN and ViT checkpoints and identical calibration labels, threshold-search budget, and hardware. Compare raw confidence, temperature scaling, failure-probability routing, and difficulty-adaptive routing on clean, corruption, and semantic/domain shifts. Keep label-aware routing as an oracle ceiling only. Report paired per-sample exit correctness, risk-coverage/outage, accuracy, FLOPs, mean/p95 latency, and separately metered device, camera, network, and server energy. Repeat seeds, include controller-training cost, and document version overlap.
